title: C Programming
description: Core C: types, control flow, functions, arrays, strings, pointers, memory and structures.

questions.prompt: Which function is the usual entry point of a C program?
questions.explanation: Execution of a hosted C program begins in main().

questions.prompt: Which header declares printf()?
questions.explanation: printf() is declared in the standard input/output header stdio.h.

questions.prompt: What does the directive #include <stdio.h> do?
choices: Inserts the header's declarations before compilation
Links the stdio library at run time
questions.explanation: The preprocessor replaces the #include line with the contents of the header file before the compiler runs.

questions.prompt: Which format specifier is commonly used to print an int in C?
questions.explanation: %d is the standard conversion specifier for an int.

questions.prompt: Which C type stores a single character?
questions.explanation: C uses char to store a character value.

questions.prompt: What is the value of 7 / 2 when both operands are int?
questions.explanation: Integer division truncates the fractional part, so 7 / 2 is 3.

questions.prompt: Which operator gives the remainder of integer division?
questions.explanation: The % operator yields the remainder, for example 7 % 2 is 1.

questions.prompt: Which statement repeats a block while a condition is true?
questions.explanation: A while loop checks its condition before each iteration.

questions.prompt: What does break do inside a loop?
questions.explanation: break exits the nearest enclosing loop or switch.

questions.prompt: In a switch statement, what happens if a case has no break?
choices: Execution falls through to the next case
questions.explanation: Without break, execution continues into the following case label (fall-through).

questions.prompt: How many times does a for-loop body run when its condition is initially false?
questions.explanation: The condition is checked before the first iteration.

questions.prompt: Which loop always executes its body at least once?
questions.explanation: do-while tests its condition after the body, so the body runs at least once.

questions.prompt: How many times does the body of for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) run?
questions.explanation: i takes the values 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4, which is five iterations.

questions.prompt: What is a function prototype used for?
questions.explanation: A prototype tells the compiler a function's name, return type and parameters.

questions.prompt: Which keyword sends a value back from a function?
questions.explanation: return ends the function and can provide a value to its caller.

questions.prompt: By default, how does C pass arguments to a function?
questions.explanation: C passes copies of argument values. To modify the caller's variable you pass its address.

questions.prompt: In C, what is the index of the first element of an array?
questions.explanation: C arrays are zero-indexed.

questions.prompt: What does int a[5]; declare?
questions.explanation: It reserves space for five consecutive int objects, indexed 0 to 4.

questions.prompt: For an array a declared in the same scope, what does sizeof(a) / sizeof(a[0]) give?
questions.explanation: Total bytes divided by bytes per element gives the element count (it does not work on a pointer parameter).

questions.prompt: Which character terminates a C string?
questions.explanation: A C string ends with the null character '\0'.

questions.prompt: Which header declares strlen()?
questions.explanation: strlen() and the other string functions are declared in string.h.

questions.prompt: What does strcmp(a, b) return when the two strings are equal?
questions.explanation: strcmp returns 0 for equal strings, a negative value if a < b and a positive value if a > b.

questions.prompt: Which operator obtains the address of a variable?
questions.explanation: The unary & operator produces the address of an object.

questions.prompt: What does a pointer variable store?
questions.explanation: A pointer stores an address referring to an object or function.

questions.prompt: If ptr is a valid int pointer, what does *ptr do?
choices: Accesses the int that ptr points to
questions.explanation: The * operator dereferences the pointer to reach the object it points to.

questions.prompt: Given int a[3] = {10, 20, 30}; int *p = a; what is *(p + 1)?
questions.explanation: Pointer arithmetic advances by one element, so p + 1 points at a[1], which is 20.

questions.prompt: Which function allocates memory dynamically from the heap?
questions.explanation: malloc() from <stdlib.h> allocates a block of heap memory.

questions.prompt: What happens if you never free() memory obtained from malloc()?
questions.explanation: Unreleased heap memory stays allocated until the program ends, which is a memory leak.

questions.prompt: Which operator accesses a member through a pointer to a struct?
questions.explanation: p->x is shorthand for (*p).x.

questions.prompt: Which keyword groups related variables under one type name?
questions.explanation: struct defines a composite type with named members.

lessons.title: Program structure and main()
objectives: Name the parts of a minimal C program
Explain why execution starts in main()
Write and read a Hello World program
lessons.body:
A C program is a collection of functions, and a hosted program always begins running in the function named main(). When main() returns, the program ends, and the returned int is handed to the operating system as an exit status. By convention 0 means success.

Lines that start with # are not ordinary C statements. They are preprocessor directives that are handled before the compiler proper sees your code. The directive #include <stdio.h> pastes in the declarations for the standard input and output functions, which is how the compiler learns what printf looks like.

Inside a function, every statement ends with a semicolon and groups of statements sit between curly braces. Text between /* and */ or after // is a comment and is ignored. Write int main(void) so the function is clearly declared as taking no arguments and returning an int.

definitions.meaning: The function where execution of a hosted C program begins.
A file of declarations, such as stdio.h, that you include so the compiler knows about library functions.
One complete instruction in C, normally ending with a semicolon.
The int returned from main(); 0 means the program finished successfully.

lessons.exampleNote: The #include line makes printf known, main() declares an int variable, printf prints text with the value substituted for %d, and return 0 reports success.
mistakes: Forgetting the semicolon after a statement, which gives an error often reported on the next line. Check the line above the one named.
Writing void main(). Use int main(void) because the standard hosted form returns int.
Leaving out #include <stdio.h> and then calling printf, which causes a warning or error about an undeclared function.

practice.q: Where does a hosted C program start running?
practice.a: In main(); the runtime calls it after setting up the program.

practice.q: What does return 0; at the end of main() tell the system?
practice.a: That the program succeeded, since 0 is the conventional success status.

exercises: Type the example, change the message, and add a second printf that prints your name on its own line.
summary: Execution starts in main().
#include pulls in declarations from a header.
Statements end with semicolons and sit in braces.
main() returns an int exit status, 0 for success.

lessons.title: Compiling and linking
objectives: List the four stages of building a C program
Run gcc with warnings enabled
Tell a compile error from a link error
lessons.body:
A C compiler turns text into a program that the computer can run. A typical build has four stages. The preprocessor handles directives such as #include and #define. The compiler then translates the result into assembly. The assembler converts assembly into object code stored in a .o file. Finally the linker combines your object files with library code, such as the C standard library, into one executable.

Most of the time a single gcc command runs all four stages for you. Add -Wall and -Wextra so the compiler warns about suspicious code, and -std=c11 to pick the language standard. The -o option names the output file.

Errors come from different stages. A syntax error or an undeclared name is reported by the compiler. A message such as undefined reference to a function means the linker could not find its definition. Read messages from the first one, because later ones are often just consequences of the first.

definitions.meaning: The first stage; it expands #include and #define before compilation.
Machine code for one source file, not yet a complete program.
The tool that joins object files and libraries into an executable.
A message about code that is legal but probably wrong; fix these too.

lessons.exampleNote: The first command compiles and links hello.c into an executable called hello with warnings on; the second line runs it from the current directory.
lessons.diagram:
hello.c
   | preprocess
   v
expanded source
   | compile
   v
assembly (.s)
   | assemble
   v
object code (.o)
   | link with libraries
   v
hello (executable)
mistakes: Ignoring warnings because the program still builds. Many warnings point at real bugs, so compile with -Wall and fix them.
Treating undefined reference as a typing error in the source. It is a link error: a function was declared but its definition or library was not supplied.
Running ./hello after a failed build and seeing an old version. Rebuild and check that the compile step printed no errors.

practice.q: Which stage turns #include lines into pasted text?
practice.a: The preprocessor, which runs before the compiler.

practice.q: An error says undefined reference to 'square'. Which stage reported it?
practice.a: The linker, because the call compiled but no definition of square was linked in.

exercises: Compile any small program once without -Wall and once with -Wall -Wextra, and compare the messages.
Create an error on purpose by deleting a semicolon, then fix it using only the compiler's first message.
summary: Build = preprocess, compile, assemble, link.
gcc can run all stages in one command.
Use -Wall -Wextra and fix warnings.
Compile errors and link errors come from different stages.

lessons.title: The preprocessor: #define and #include
objectives: Define constants and function-like macros
Explain why macro arguments need parentheses
Describe what an include guard does
lessons.body:
Before compilation, the preprocessor rewrites your source text. It does not understand C types or expressions; it only copies and replaces text. #include pastes in another file. Angle brackets such as <stdio.h> search the system header directories, while quotes such as "mine.h" look in your project first.

#define NAME value creates an object-like macro, a named constant that is replaced everywhere before compilation. A function-like macro takes arguments, as in SQUARE(x). Because the replacement is plain text, you must wrap every parameter and the whole body in parentheses, otherwise operator precedence can change the meaning.

Conditional directives such as #ifdef, #ifndef and #endif keep or drop code at compile time. A header usually starts with #ifndef NAME, then #define NAME, and ends with #endif. This include guard stops the header being processed twice in the same file. For simple constants, a const variable or an enum is often safer because the compiler checks its type.

definitions.meaning: A name that the preprocessor replaces with other text.
The #ifndef/#define/#endif pattern that prevents a header being included twice.
Choosing which code reaches the compiler using directives such as #ifdef.

lessons.exampleNote: This prints 16 10. Because of the parentheses, SQUARE(n + 1) becomes ((n + 1) * (n + 1)), which is 16; without them it would become n + 1 * n + 1, which is 7.
lessons.diagram:
SQUARE(n + 1)
   |  text replacement
   v
((n + 1) * (n + 1))      = 16

without parentheses: x * x
n + 1 * n + 1            = 7
mistakes: Writing #define SQUARE(x) x * x. Parenthesise each parameter and the whole body.
Passing an expression with side effects such as SQUARE(i++). The argument is evaluated twice, which is undefined behaviour. Use a real function instead.
Putting a semicolon at the end of #define MAX 10;. The semicolon becomes part of the replacement and breaks expressions.

practice.q: What does #define PI 3.14 do?
practice.a: It makes the preprocessor replace the token PI with 3.14 before compilation.

practice.q: Why do headers have include guards?
practice.a: To stop duplicate declarations when the same header is reached more than once.

exercises: Define a macro MAX(a, b) with correct parentheses and test it with MAX(2 + 3, 4).
Write a small header file with an include guard and include it twice in a program.
summary: The preprocessor works on text, not types.
#include copies a file; #define replaces tokens.
Parenthesise macro parameters and bodies.
Include guards prevent double inclusion.

lessons.title: Data types and format specifiers
objectives: Choose a suitable type for a value
Match printf format specifiers to types
Use sizeof to inspect type sizes
lessons.body:
Every variable in C has a type that decides what values it can hold and how much memory it uses. The basic types are char for a single character, int for whole numbers, float and double for numbers with a fractional part, and void for no value. Modifiers such as short, long, signed and unsigned change the range.

The exact size of int, long and the rest depends on the platform, so never assume it. The language only guarantees that sizeof(char) is 1. Use sizeof to check on your machine, or include <stdint.h> for exact-width types such as int32_t. The header <limits.h> gives the actual minimum and maximum values.

printf needs a format specifier that matches the argument type: %d for int, %u for unsigned int, %ld for long, %f for float or double, %c for char, %s for a string and %zu for the size_t value produced by sizeof. A mismatch is undefined behaviour, so enable warnings. Declare a variable and give it a value before you read it.

definitions.meaning: The kind of value a variable holds, which fixes its size and allowed operations.
The %-code in printf that says how to print an argument.
An operator giving the size in bytes of a type or object, as a size_t.
A type modifier meaning the value is never negative.

lessons.exampleNote: The first printf prints 20 36.5 A, with %.1f keeping one decimal place. The second reports the size of int on your machine, commonly 4 bytes.
lessons.diagram:
type      printf    example
char      %c        'A'
int       %d        42
unsigned  %u        42u
long      %ld       42L
float     %f        3.5f
double    %f        3.5
char[]    %s        "hi"
size_t    %zu       sizeof x
mistakes: Printing a double with %d. The output is garbage or undefined; use %f.
Assuming int is always 4 bytes. Check sizeof or use int32_t when the exact size matters.
Using a variable before assigning it. A local variable holds an indeterminate value until you initialise it.

practice.q: Which specifier prints a char as a character?
practice.a: %c; %d would print its numeric code instead.

practice.q: What type does sizeof produce and how is it printed?
practice.a: size_t, printed with %zu.

exercises: Print sizeof for char, short, int, long, float and double on your machine.
Store 65 in a char and print it with %c and with %d, then explain both outputs.
summary: Each variable has a type that fixes size and range.
Sizes beyond char vary by platform; use sizeof.
Match format specifiers to argument types.
Initialise variables before reading them.

lessons.title: Operators and integer division
objectives: Predict the result of integer division and remainder
Use relational and logical operators correctly
Avoid the = versus == mistake
lessons.body:
The arithmetic operators are + - * / and %. When both operands of / are integers, the result is also an integer: the fractional part is discarded, truncating toward zero. So 7 / 2 is 3 and -7 / 2 is -3. The % operator gives the remainder, and its sign follows the left operand, so -7 % 2 is -1. If one operand is a double, the other is converted and you get real division, so 7 / 2.0 is 3.5. Dividing by zero is undefined behaviour for integers.

Relational operators (< <= > >= == !=) and logical operators (&& || !) produce 1 for true and 0 for false. In a condition, any nonzero value counts as true. && and || stop early, so the right side runs only if it is needed.

Operators have precedence: * / % bind tighter than + -. Add parentheses whenever you are unsure. The single = assigns a value, while == compares; writing if (x = 5) assigns 5 and is always true.

definitions.meaning: Division of two integers; the result is an integer with the fraction discarded.
The % operator, which gives the remainder of integer division.
The rule deciding which operator is applied first in an expression.
Skipping the right operand of && or || when the left already decides the result.

lessons.exampleNote: The first line prints 3 1 using integer division and remainder. Casting a to double before dividing makes real division, so the second line prints 3.5.
mistakes: Expecting 7 / 2 to be 3.5. Make at least one operand a double, for example 7 / 2.0 or (double)a / b.
Writing (double)(a / b) and still getting 3. The division already happened in integers; cast an operand first.
Typing = inside a condition. Use == to compare and turn on -Wall so the compiler warns.

practice.q: What are 9 / 4 and 9 % 4 for ints?
practice.a: 2 and 1, because 4 goes into 9 twice with remainder 1.

practice.q: What does the expression 3 > 2 evaluate to in C?
practice.a: 1, since relational operators give 1 for true.

exercises: Write a program that reads two ints from variables and prints their quotient and remainder.
Predict, then run, the value of 2 + 3 * 4 and (2 + 3) * 4.
summary: Integer / integer drops the fraction.
% gives the remainder; its sign follows the left operand.
Conditions treat nonzero as true.
= assigns, == compares.

lessons.title: Reading input with scanf
objectives: Read ints and doubles with scanf
Explain why scanf needs the address of a variable
Check scanf's return value
lessons.body:
scanf reads formatted text from standard input and stores the converted values into variables. Because C passes arguments by value, scanf cannot change your variable unless you give it the variable's address, so you write &age. The format string says what to expect: %d for int, %f for float, %lf for double (note the l, which is required in scanf), and %c for a character.

scanf returns the number of values it successfully stored. Always test it: if the user types letters where a number is expected, the return value is smaller than you hoped and the variable keeps its old value. Whitespace in the format, such as the space in "%d %d", skips any amount of spaces and newlines. A space before %c, as in " %c", skips the leftover newline from a previous line.

For %s, the address is the array itself, no & needed, and you should give a width, such as %19s for a 20-byte array, so a long word cannot overflow it. When you want whole lines including spaces, fgets is usually the better tool.

definitions.meaning: The standard input stream, normally the keyboard.
The count of items successfully converted, or EOF if input ended first.
Gives scanf the location where it should store the value.

lessons.exampleNote: Typing 20 1.75 prints 20 years, 1.75 m. The if checks that scanf stored both values, so bad input is reported instead of silently using garbage.
lessons.diagram:
input text:  20 1.75\n
             -- ----
             %d %lf
scanf("%d %lf", &age, &height)
returns 2 if both were converted
mistakes: Forgetting &, as in scanf("%d", age). scanf then writes through a bad address. Pass &age.
Using %f for a double in scanf. It stores a float-sized value; use %lf for double.
Reading a char right after a number and getting the newline. Put a space before %c in the format.

practice.q: Why does scanf need &x and not x?
practice.a: It must change the caller's variable, and C passes copies, so it needs the address.

practice.q: What does scanf return for input 'abc' with format %d?
practice.a: 0, because no value could be converted.

exercises: Write a program that asks for two integers and prints their sum, rejecting bad input.
Read a word with %19s into char name[20] and print it back.
summary: scanf needs addresses: &x for numbers.
Use %lf for double in scanf.
Check that the return value equals the number of items.
Give %s a width to avoid overflow.

lessons.title: Conditionals: if, else and switch
objectives: Write if, else if and else chains
Use switch with break and default
Explain fall-through
lessons.body:
Control flow decides which statements run. An if statement tests a condition; if it is nonzero the following statement or block runs, otherwise the else part runs. Chain several tests with else if, and the first true branch wins. Use braces even for one statement, which prevents bugs when you add a second line later.

A switch compares one integer expression (an int, char or enum value) against case labels, each of which must be a constant. Strings and floating-point values cannot be switch expressions. When a case matches, execution continues until a break or the closing brace. Without break, it falls through into the next case. That is occasionally useful, for example to give several labels the same action, but it is usually a bug, so add a comment when you do it on purpose.

Add a default case to handle values you did not list. For ranges, such as marks between 40 and 59, an if chain is the better choice than a switch.

definitions.meaning: An expression whose value, zero or nonzero, selects a branch.
Continuing from one switch case into the next because there is no break.
The switch label that runs when no case matches.

lessons.exampleNote: With marks 55 the else if branch prints Pass, and day 3 prints Wed. Each case ends in break so no other case runs.
lessons.diagram:
marks >= 40 ?
       /          \
    true         false
     |             |
 print Pass   print Try again
       \          /
     next statement
mistakes: Forgetting break in a switch, so several cases run. Add break unless fall-through is intended.
Writing if (x = 0) instead of if (x == 0). Compile with -Wall to catch it.
Putting a semicolon right after the if condition, which makes the body empty. Remove it.

practice.q: In a switch with no break in case 1, what runs after case 1's code?
practice.a: The code of the next case, because execution falls through.

practice.q: Can a switch use a string as its expression?
practice.a: No; it needs an integer-type expression with constant case labels.

exercises: Write a program that prints a letter grade for marks using else if.
Use a switch on a char to print Vowel for a, e, i, o, u by sharing one action between labels.
summary: if/else if/else picks the first true branch.
switch needs integer constants and break.
Missing break causes fall-through.
Use braces and a default case.

lessons.title: Loops: for, while and do-while
objectives: Choose between for, while and do-while
Trace a loop by hand
Avoid off-by-one errors and infinite loops
lessons.body:
Loops repeat a block of code. A for loop puts the setup, test and update in one line: for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) starts i at 0, checks i < 5 before each pass, and adds 1 after each pass. It is the natural choice when you know how many times to repeat. A while loop only has a test, and is better when the count is not known in advance. A do-while checks its test after the body, so the body always runs at least once, which suits menus and input checks.

Inside any loop, break leaves the nearest enclosing loop immediately, and continue skips the rest of the current pass and moves to the next test. If a loop never stops, check that something in the body changes the variable used by the condition.

A very common bug is the off-by-one error. A loop from 0 while i < n runs exactly n times; using i <= n runs n + 1 times, and with an array it reads one element too many.

definitions.meaning: One pass through the body of a loop.
A variable, often i, that tracks the pass number.
A loop whose condition never becomes false.

lessons.exampleNote: The for loop adds 1 to 5 and gives sum 15. The do-while prints 3 2 1, then the final line prints sum=15.
lessons.diagram:
for (init; cond; update) body

1) init     (once)
2) cond     false -> leave loop
3) body
4) update   then back to step 2

do { body } while (cond);
body first, then test
mistakes: Using <= with a zero-based count, which runs one time too many. Use i < n for n repetitions.
Adding a semicolon after for (...); which turns the body into an empty statement. Delete the semicolon.
Forgetting to update the counter in a while loop, so it never ends. Make sure the body moves toward the exit.

practice.q: How many times does for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) run its body?
practice.a: 3 times, with i equal to 0, 1 and 2.

practice.q: Which loop runs its body once even if the condition is false?
practice.a: do-while, because it tests after the body.

exercises: Print the multiplication table of 7 using a for loop.
Use a while loop to count how many times you can halve 100 before reaching 1 using integer division.
summary: for suits a known count; while an unknown count.
do-while always runs at least once.
break exits; continue skips to the next test.
i < n repeats n times from 0.

lessons.title: Functions, prototypes and parameters
objectives: Declare, define and call a function
Explain why C passes arguments by value
Use a pointer parameter to modify a caller's variable
lessons.body:
A function packages a task under a name. It has a return type, a name and a parameter list, then a body in braces. The return statement sends a value back to the caller and ends the function. A function with return type void returns nothing.

In C99 and later you must declare a function before you call it. A prototype, such as int add(int a, int b);, tells the compiler the name, parameter types and return type, so calls can be checked. Put prototypes near the top of the file or in a header, and the definition anywhere after.

C passes arguments by value: the function receives copies, so changing a parameter does not change the caller's variable. To let a function modify a caller's variable, pass its address and dereference the pointer inside the function. Variables declared inside a function are local, visible only there, and they disappear when the function returns.

definitions.meaning: A declaration giving a function's return type, name and parameter types.
The variable named in a function definition that receives a value.
The value you pass in a call.
Giving the function a copy, so the original is unchanged.

lessons.exampleNote: The first printf shows 5 because bump only changed its copy. After bump_ptr(&n) the variable really changes, so the second line prints 6 5.
mistakes: Expecting a function to change its argument. Pass a pointer, as in swap(&a, &b), when it must.
Calling a function before declaring it. Add a prototype above main().
Returning the address of a local variable. The variable is gone after the function returns; return a value or use caller-supplied memory.

practice.q: Does void f(int x) { x = 9; } change the caller's variable?
practice.a: No, x is a copy of the argument.

practice.q: What does a prototype let the compiler do?
practice.a: Check the number and types of arguments in calls before the definition is seen.

exercises: Write int max2(int a, int b) with a prototype and test it from main().
Write void swap(int *a, int *b) and show that it swaps two variables.
summary: Functions have a return type, name, parameters and body.
Declare with a prototype before use.
Arguments are copied; pass pointers to modify originals.
Locals vanish when the function returns.

lessons.title: Recursion
objectives: Identify the base case and recursive case
Trace a recursive call on the call stack
Explain why missing base cases overflow the stack
lessons.body:
A recursive function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem. Every correct recursive function has two parts. The base case returns an answer directly and stops the recursion. The recursive case calls the function again with a value that moves closer to the base case.

Each call gets its own stack frame holding its parameters and local variables. The frames pile up on the call stack as the calls go deeper, then are removed one by one as each call returns. The stack has limited size, so if a base case is missing or never reached, the calls continue until the stack overflows and the program crashes.

Recursion is neat for naturally nested problems such as factorials, trees and divide-and-conquer. A loop is often faster and uses less memory for simple repetition. Also watch the result size: factorial(13) does not fit in a 32-bit int, so use a wider type such as unsigned long long for larger inputs.

definitions.meaning: The input for which the function returns directly without calling itself.
The part where the function calls itself on a smaller problem.
The block of stack memory for one function call.
A crash caused by using up the call stack, often by endless recursion.

lessons.exampleNote: factorial(5) calls factorial(4), and so on down to factorial(1), which returns 1. The results multiply on the way back, giving 120.
lessons.diagram:
call stack (top = newest)
+-----------------------+
| factorial(1) -> 1     |
| factorial(2) waits    |
| factorial(3) waits    |
| main                  |
+-----------------------+
returns: 1, then 2*1=2, then 3*2=6
mistakes: Forgetting the base case, so the function never stops. Write the base case first.
Calling with an argument that does not approach the base case, for example factorial(n) instead of factorial(n - 1).
Using int for large factorials. The value overflows; use unsigned long long and limit n.

practice.q: What is the base case in factorial above?
practice.a: n <= 1, which returns 1 without another call.

practice.q: What happens if the base case is missing?
practice.a: Calls keep stacking until the stack overflows and the program crashes.

exercises: Write a recursive function that adds the digits of a non-negative integer.
Trace factorial(4) on paper, drawing each stack frame.
summary: Every recursion needs a base case and progress toward it.
Each call has its own stack frame.
Endless recursion overflows the stack.
A loop can replace simple recursion.

lessons.title: Arrays
objectives: Declare and initialise an array
Use zero-based indices safely
Compute the element count with sizeof
lessons.body:
An array holds a fixed number of elements of the same type in one contiguous block of memory. int marks[3] declares room for three ints. The index starts at 0, so the valid indices are 0 to length minus 1. Elements sit right next to each other, which is why access by index is fast.

C does not check bounds. Reading or writing marks[3] in a three-element array is undefined behaviour: it may crash, print garbage or silently corrupt another variable. You must keep track of the valid range yourself.

You can initialise an array with braces. If you give fewer values than elements, the rest become zero. Where the array is declared, sizeof(a) / sizeof(a[0]) gives the number of elements. This trick fails inside a function that receives the array as a parameter, because the parameter is really a pointer, so pass the length separately. Also, an array cannot be assigned or compared with = and ==; copy elements in a loop or with memcpy.

definitions.meaning: The position of an element, starting at 0.
Stored one after another with no gaps.
Using an index outside the array, which is undefined behaviour.
The brace list that gives the starting values.

lessons.exampleNote: The count is computed as 3, the loop visits indices 0 to 2, and the program prints 3 items, total 240.
mistakes: Using marks[3] as the last element of a three-element array. The last valid index is 2.
Using sizeof on an array parameter inside a function. It gives the pointer size; pass the length as an argument.
Trying b = a to copy an array. Copy each element or use memcpy.

practice.q: What is the last valid index of int a[10]?
practice.a: 9, since indices run from 0 to length minus 1.

practice.q: What does int a[5] = {1, 2}; store in a[4]?
practice.a: 0, because missing initialisers are zero.

exercises: Write a program that finds the largest value in an array of five ints.
Print the array in reverse order using a loop that counts down.
summary: Arrays are fixed-size, contiguous and same-typed.
Indices run from 0 to n - 1.
C does not check bounds.
sizeof(a) / sizeof(a[0]) works only where the array is declared.

lessons.title: Strings and string.h
objectives: Explain the null terminator
Use strlen and strcmp correctly
Copy text without overflowing a buffer
lessons.body:
C has no string type. A string is a char array whose last character is the null character '\0', which has the value 0. A literal such as "Cat" occupies four bytes: 'C', 'a', 't' and the terminator. The functions in <string.h> depend on that terminator to know where the text ends.

strlen returns the number of characters before the terminator, so it does not count it. strcmp compares two strings and returns 0 when they are equal, a negative number if the first is smaller and a positive number if it is larger; the exact values are not guaranteed to be -1 and 1. You cannot compare strings with ==, because that compares addresses.

strcpy and strcat do not check the size of the destination. If it is too small, the program overflows the buffer and misbehaves. Make the buffer large enough for the text plus one byte for '\0', or use snprintf(buf, sizeof buf, "%s", src), which never writes past the buffer. Do not modify a string literal through a char pointer; store text you want to change in an array.

definitions.meaning: The character '\0' that marks the end of a C string.
Returns the length of a string, not counting the terminator.
Writing past the end of an array, which is undefined behaviour.
Text in double quotes in source code, stored as read-only data.

lessons.exampleNote: snprintf copies the text safely into copy, strlen reports 9, and strcmp returns 0 so the program prints equal. The output is LearnMate 9 and then equal.
mistakes: Comparing with if (a == b). That compares addresses; use strcmp(a, b) == 0.
Making the buffer exactly as long as the text, with no room for '\0'. Allow one extra byte.
Changing a literal through char *p = "abc"; p[0] = 'x'; which is undefined. Use char p[] = "abc"; instead.

practice.q: What does strlen("Cat") return, and what does sizeof("Cat") give?
practice.a: 3 and 4, because the terminator counts for sizeof but not strlen.

practice.q: What does strcmp return for identical strings?

exercises: Write a function that counts the vowels in a string.
Reverse a string in place using two indices that move toward each other.
summary: A string is a char array ending with '\0'.
strlen excludes the terminator; the array needs one more byte.
Use strcmp, not ==, to compare.
Use bounded copies to avoid overflow.

lessons.title: Pointers
objectives: Declare a pointer and take an address with &
Dereference a pointer with *
Avoid NULL and uninitialised pointers
lessons.body:
A pointer is a variable whose value is the memory address of another object. Declaring int *ptr says that ptr can hold the address of an int. The address-of operator & gives the address of a variable, so ptr = &value makes ptr point to value.

The * operator has two jobs. In a declaration it marks a pointer type. In an expression, *ptr dereferences the pointer: it means the object that ptr points to, so you can read it or assign to it. Writing *ptr = 20 changes value itself.

Pointers are powerful and dangerous. A pointer that was never initialised holds a random address, and dereferencing it is undefined behaviour. Set pointers to NULL when they point to nothing and test them before use, because dereferencing NULL normally crashes. Note that in int *a, b; only a is a pointer and b is a plain int. Pointers let functions modify the caller's variables and are the basis of dynamic memory and arrays.

definitions.meaning: A variable that stores the address of another object.
Using * to access the object a pointer points to.
A special pointer value meaning it points to no object.
The & operator, which yields the address of a variable.

lessons.exampleNote: The first line prints 10 by reading through ptr. After *ptr = 20, value is 20. The last line prints the address, which differs from run to run.
lessons.diagram:
int value = 10;
int *ptr = &value;

  value            ptr
+--------+      +--------+
|   10   | <--- | 0x1000 |
+--------+      +--------+
 at 0x1000      holds that address
(address shown is only illustrative)
mistakes: Dereferencing an uninitialised or NULL pointer. Initialise to a valid address or NULL and check before use.
Thinking int *a, b; makes two pointers. Only a is one; write int *a, *b; for two.
Confusing ptr with *ptr. ptr is the address; *ptr is the value stored there.

practice.q: If int x = 4; int *p = &x; what is *p?
practice.a: 4, the value of x that p points to.

practice.q: After *p = 9; what is x?
practice.a: 9, because p points to x.

exercises: Write a swap function that exchanges two ints through pointers.
Print a variable and its address, then print the value read through a pointer to it.
summary: A pointer stores an address.
& takes an address; * dereferences.
Initialise pointers or set them to NULL.
Pointers let functions change caller variables.

lessons.title: Pointers and arrays together
objectives: Explain how an array name becomes a pointer
Use pointer arithmetic to reach elements
Pass an array and its length to a function
lessons.body:
In most expressions, the name of an array is converted to a pointer to its first element. So after int v[4]; and int *p = v;, the pointer p holds the address of v[0]. This conversion is often called array decay.

Pointer arithmetic is scaled by the size of the pointed-to type. p + 1 is the address of the next int, not the next byte, so *(p + 2) is the third element. In fact, the subscript v[i] is defined as *(v + i), and that is why p[2] also works when p is a pointer.

Because an array decays when passed to a function, a function that receives int a[] really receives a pointer. It cannot tell how many elements there are, so pass the length as a second parameter. Use const when the function only reads the data. Remember that an array is not a pointer: sizeof v is the size of the whole array, while sizeof p is just the pointer size, and you cannot assign a new address to an array name. Never dereference a pointer that goes past the end of the array. Pointing one element past the end is allowed, but reading it is not.

definitions.meaning: The automatic conversion of an array name to a pointer to its first element.
Adding or subtracting integers to a pointer, scaled by the element size.
A parameter promising the function will not modify the data it points to.

lessons.exampleNote: The first line prints 30 30 30 because all three expressions name the third element. sum receives a pointer and a count, and the second line prints 100.
mistakes: Using sizeof on an array parameter to get its length. It returns the pointer size; pass the length explicitly.
Thinking p + 1 adds one byte. It adds sizeof(*p) bytes, so it lands on the next element.
Reading *(p + n) for an n-element array. Only n - 1 is the last valid element.

practice.q: If int v[3] = {5, 6, 7}; int *p = v; what is *(p + 1)?
practice.a: 6, the second element.

practice.q: Why must a function taking int *a also take a length?
practice.a: The pointer carries no size information.

exercises: Write int max_of(const int *a, size_t n) and call it with an array.
Walk through an array using a pointer that increments until it reaches v + n.
summary: An array name decays to a pointer to element 0.
a[i] means *(a + i).
Pointer arithmetic is scaled by element size.
Pass array length separately to functions.

lessons.title: Dynamic memory: malloc and free
objectives: Allocate and release heap memory
Check allocation results for NULL
Recognise leaks, double frees and use after free
lessons.body:
Local variables live on the stack and disappear when their function returns. When you need memory whose size is chosen at run time, or that must outlive the function, you ask the heap through <stdlib.h>. malloc(n) returns a pointer to n uninitialised bytes. calloc(count, size) returns zeroed memory. realloc resizes a block and may move it. free hands the block back.

Rules to follow every time. Compute the size with sizeof of the pointed-to object, as in malloc(5 * sizeof *p). Check the result for NULL because allocation can fail. Free each block exactly once, and never touch it afterwards, since a pointer to freed memory is dangling. Setting the pointer to NULL after free helps catch mistakes.

If you lose the last pointer to a block without freeing it, the memory is leaked and stays reserved until the program ends. For realloc, save the result in a temporary pointer first, because on failure it returns NULL and the original block is still yours. In C you do not need to cast the result of malloc.

definitions.meaning: The pool of memory managed with malloc and free, whose blocks live until freed.
Allocated memory that is never freed and can no longer be reached.
A pointer to memory that has already been freed.
Calling free twice on the same block, which is undefined behaviour.

lessons.exampleNote: The program asks for room for five ints, checks it succeeded, fills them with squares and prints 16. It then frees the block and clears the pointer.
lessons.diagram:
stack                  heap
+-----------+         +---------+
| int *p  --|-------->| 5 ints  |
+-----------+         |(malloc) |
 vanishes when        +---------+
 function returns      stays until
                       free(p)
mistakes: Using memory after free(p). Set p = NULL afterwards and do not read through it.
Calling free twice on the same pointer. Free once; free(NULL) is harmless, which is another reason to reset to NULL.
Writing p = realloc(p, n) directly. If it fails you lose the old block; use a temporary and check it.

practice.q: Which function gives zero-initialised memory?
practice.a: calloc.

practice.q: What is the problem with never calling free on a malloc'd block?
practice.a: A memory leak, the memory stays reserved until the program ends.

exercises: Ask the user for n, allocate an int array of that size, fill and print it, then free it.
Grow an array from 3 to 6 ints with realloc using a temporary pointer.
summary: malloc, calloc and realloc get heap memory; free returns it.
Always check for NULL.
Free exactly once and never use freed memory.
Lost pointers cause leaks.

lessons.title: Structures, unions and enums
objectives: Define a struct and access members with . and ->
Explain how union and enum differ from struct
Use typedef to shorten type names
lessons.body:
A struct groups related variables, called members, under one type. The members can have different types, so a student can have an int id, a char grade and a name array together. Use the dot operator for a struct variable, as in s.id, and the arrow operator for a pointer to a struct, where p->id is shorthand for (*p).id.

Structs can be copied with =, passed to functions and returned, but they cannot be compared with ==. Compare member by member. A char array member cannot be assigned with =; copy text with strcpy or snprintf. Do not forget the semicolon after the closing brace of the definition.

A union looks like a struct but all members share the same storage, so it is as large as its largest member, and you should read the member you most recently wrote. An enum defines names for integer constants, starting at 0 unless you set values. typedef creates a shorter alias, such as typedef struct Student Student;.

definitions.meaning: A variable that belongs to a struct or union.
->, used to reach a member through a pointer to a struct.
A type whose members share one block of memory.
A type with named integer constants.

lessons.exampleNote: Changing p->id changes s.id because p points to s, so the line prints 2 A 1. GREEN is the second enum constant, so its value is 1.
mistakes: Using . on a pointer or -> on a plain struct. Dot for variables, arrow for pointers.
Comparing two structs with ==. It does not compile; compare members.
Forgetting the semicolon after a struct definition, which causes confusing errors.

practice.q: If p points to a struct Student, how do you read its id?
practice.a: p->id, or equivalently (*p).id.

practice.q: What is the value of BLUE in enum Color { RED, GREEN, BLUE }?
practice.a: 2, since values start at 0 and increase by 1.

exercises: Define a struct Point with x and y, and write a function that prints a Point through a pointer.
Create an enum for four weekdays and use it in a switch.
summary: A struct groups members of different types.
Use . for variables and -> for pointers.
A union's members share storage.
An enum gives names to integer constants.

lessons.title: File handling
objectives: Open, use and close a file safely
Choose the correct open mode
Read a text file line by line
lessons.body:
File input and output uses a FILE pointer and functions from <stdio.h>. fopen(name, mode) opens a file and returns a FILE pointer, or NULL if it fails, for example when the file does not exist. Always check for NULL and report the problem, perror is handy for that. When you finish, call fclose so buffered data is written out and resources are released.

The mode string decides what is allowed. "r" reads an existing file, "w" creates a file or erases an existing one, and "a" appends to the end. Add b, as in "rb" or "wb", for binary files. fprintf and fscanf work like printf and scanf but take the FILE pointer first and handle text. fread and fwrite move raw bytes, which suits binary data.

To read a text file one line at a time, loop on fgets, which returns NULL at the end of the file. Avoid using feof as the loop condition, because it only becomes true after a read has already failed, which gives one extra iteration.

definitions.meaning: The type that represents an open stream; you only hold a pointer to it.
The string in fopen saying whether to read, write or append, text or binary.
Data held in memory until it is flushed or the file is closed.

lessons.exampleNote: The program writes two lines to notes.txt, closes it, reopens it for reading and prints read: Hello and read: LearnMate. Each fopen result is checked.
lessons.diagram:
write:
program --fprintf--> fp --> notes.txt

read:
program <--fgets---- fp <-- notes.txt

modes: "r" read   "w" write/erase
       "a" append   +b = binary
mistakes: Not checking fopen for NULL, which leads to a crash on the first use. Test and handle the failure.
Using mode "w" on a file you meant to keep. It erases the old contents; use "a" to add to the end.
Forgetting fclose, so buffered data may never reach the disk. Close every file you open.

practice.q: What does fopen return on failure?
practice.a: NULL.

practice.q: What is the difference between modes w and a?
practice.a: w erases existing content first; a keeps it and adds at the end.

exercises: Write a program that saves three numbers to a file, then reads them back and prints their sum.
Count the lines in a text file with fgets.
summary: fopen returns NULL on failure; check it.
Mode r, w or a chooses read, write or append.
Close files with fclose.
fgets reads a line at a time.

lessons.title: Debugging common C errors
objectives: Read a compiler message for file, line and cause
List common causes of C bugs
Use warnings and tools to find a crash
lessons.body:
Start with the compiler's message, because it names the file, line and column and describes the problem. Fix the first error and rebuild; later errors are often side effects of the first. A missing semicolon is usually reported on the line after the real mistake, so look one line up.

Common causes of trouble are mismatched braces, wrong format specifiers, array indices out of range, uninitialised variables, NULL or dangling pointers, missing prototypes and using = instead of ==. Compile with -Wall -Wextra and treat warnings as real problems.

A segmentation fault means the program touched memory it may not use, often through a bad pointer or an out-of-range index. Compile with -g and -fsanitize=address, which are supported by gcc and clang, to get a report naming the line. A debugger such as gdb can show where the crash happened, and simple printf statements help you see variable values. Always shrink the failing code to the smallest example that still fails, and change one thing at a time.

definitions.meaning: A crash caused by an invalid memory access.
A diagnostic about suspicious but legal code.
A tool such as gdb that lets you pause a program and inspect it.
A compiler option that adds run-time checks and reports memory errors.

lessons.exampleNote: The buggy loop runs with i equal to 3 and reads outside the array. Changing <= to < keeps every index in the range 0 to 2.
lessons.diagram:
main.c:5:20: error: expected ';'
  |    | |   |      |
 file line col kind  message

A missing ';' is often reported
on the NEXT line - look above it.
mistakes: Fixing the last error first. Start with the first message and rebuild.
Ignoring warnings because the program runs. Treat them as likely bugs.
Changing many things at once, so you cannot tell which change helped. Make one change per test.

practice.q: What does a segmentation fault usually mean?
practice.a: The program accessed invalid memory, for example through a bad pointer or an out-of-range index.

practice.q: Why compile with -Wall?
practice.a: It enables warnings that reveal many bugs before running.

exercises: Take a program with an off-by-one loop bug and find it using -fsanitize=address.
Write a program with an uninitialised variable and see which warning -Wall -Wextra produces.
summary: Read the first compiler message first.
Compile with -Wall -Wextra and fix warnings.
Segfaults come from invalid memory access.
Reduce the failing code and change one thing at a time.
